A passage from Sefer HaBahir (5219) on the offering (terumah) lifted in prayer. The Garden, the pillar and midnight (5226-5231). The staff, Marah and the rock (5232-5267).

family: The Zohar, volume III: the One made whole below
title: The Zohar on Vayikra, Bamidbar and Devarim, line by line: the One made whole below, and the Lamp that is all its lights
abstract: Volume 3 of the Zohar says two things about the One, and it keeps both. First, G-d is One and does not change. He "surrounds all worlds and fills all worlds." He "grasps all and nothing grasps Him." Every name is only a title for His deeds toward us. The Idra gives the rule behind all of this: the Ancient One and the Small Face are "all one," and "it is from our side that they differ."

family: The Zohar, volume III: the One made whole below
title: Zohar, volume 3, part 1: Vayikra (lines 1-449)
abstract: Vayikra is the book of offerings, and the Zohar reads every offering as one thing: bringing near. A korban (offering) is a drawing close, and what is drawn close is not only a person to G-d but the powers above to each other, until they are one. That idea runs the whole range.

family: The Zohar, volume III: the One made whole below
title: Zohar, volume 3, part 2: Tzav, Shmini, Tazria, Metzora (lines 450-1011)
abstract: These four parashot are about fire, the priest, the Eighth Day, forbidden food, birth, and the leper. The Zohar turns each into a teaching about the soul and the Presence. Three threads run through it. The offering rises to Ein Sof, and the will is what rises. The burnt offering (olah) is the Shechinah going up; the smoke is "the will of all" (450-474). The deed below wakes the deed above.

family: The Zohar, volume III: the One made whole below
title: Zohar, volume 3, part 3: Achrei Mot (lines 1012-1424)
abstract: Achrei Mot is the parasha of Yom Kippur, and the Zohar reads it through one story: Rabbi Shimon and the companions walk to Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, and on the way and at his table they open the service of the day. The high priest's entry into the Holy of Holies becomes a teaching about uniting the Name, about times of favor, about the scapegoat that turns the accuser into a defender, and about teshuvah as the depth from which one calls.

family: The Zohar, volume III: the One made whole below
title: Zohar, volume 3, part 4: Kedoshim, Emor, Behar, Bechukotai (lines 1425-2044)
abstract: These parashot hold the holiness code, the priests, the calendar of festivals, the Sabbatical year and the blessings and curses. The Zohar reads them as the year of a soul: a person made "one" by holiness, a week that ends in the King's wedding, festivals that are invitations to a guest, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur as a trial where the King's love for His children overcomes His love of justice, Sukkot as sitting "in the shade of faith", and the curses of Bechukotai read as the King who goes …

family: The Zohar, volume III: the One made whole below
title: Zohar, volume 3, part 5: Bamidbar and Nasso (lines 2045-2320)
abstract: Bamidbar counts Israel; Nasso holds the sotah, the nazir and the priestly blessing. The Zohar builds a daily life out of them. The strongest material here is about the morning and the night: depositing the soul at night, the order of the morning prayer, the falling on the face after the Amidah as a real giving-over of the self, and the priestly blessing as the hour when the Hidden is revealed and "whisper and silence" fill the worlds.

family: The Zohar, volume III: the One made whole below
title: Zohar, volume 3, part 6: the Idra Rabba in Naso (lines 2321-2684)
abstract: The Idra Rabba ("the great gathering") is a single scene. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai calls ten companions into a field, sits them in a circle, and asks each in turn to stand and "set in order" one feature of a vast face. First comes the face of Atika, the Ancient One, also called Arikh Anpin, the Long Face: His skull, the dew that drips from it, His hair, His forehead, His one open eye, His nose, and the thirteen parts of His white beard.

family: The Zohar, volume III: the One made whole below
title: Zohar, volume 3, part 7: Beha'alotcha and Sh'lach (lines 2685-3182)
abstract: Beha'alotcha opens with the lamps and incense of the priest, and holds the Zohar's most famous teaching on how to read the Torah: the story is a garment, the commandments are the body, and the soul of the Torah lies under both (2742-2748). It goes on to the ark that "turns its face" to Israel (2812-2816), and to Moshe's cry "kill me" read as a lesson about anger (2820-2833).

family: The Zohar, volume III: the One made whole below
title: Zohar, volume 3, part 8: Korach, Chukat and Balak (lines 3183-3839)
abstract: Korach is about peace and division. The Name of G-d is "Peace," and whoever splits peace splits the Name (3187-3190). It also teaches how the priest's quiet incense calms anger (3202-3209), and how to include the left in the right (3210-3216). Chukat holds the red heifer (3260-3276), the deaths of Miriam, Aaron and Moshe as moon, arm and sun (3277-3310), and a sharp teaching on who knows how to "call" G-d in prayer (3317-3325). Balak is one of the longest sections in the volume.

family: The Zohar, volume III: the One made whole below
title: Zohar, volume 3, part 9: Pinchas, first half (lines 3840-4287)
abstract: Pinchas opens with the zealot's reward and turns fast to the inner life. The main story. Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Yosi rise at midnight to learn. A shadow walks through the house, and it is the soul of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair (3923-3972). Later Rabbi Shimon meets the living Rabbi Pinchas on the road, under a tree by a spring, with an eagle and a rose (3997-4237). The Raya Mehemna layer.

family: The Zohar, volume III: the One made whole below
title: Zohar, volume 3, part 10: Pinchas, second half (lines 4288-4734)
abstract: The Torah here lists the daily, Shabbos, new-moon and festival offerings. The Zohar and the Raya Mehemna turn each into a teaching about prayer and the inner life: - the daily burnt offering as a prayer that rises to the Infinite (4674-4677); - Shabbos and the extra soul given to each person by his level (4407-4411); - the new moon and her smallness (4510-4529); - the hind of the dawn (4530-4541); - Pesach, chametz and matzah (4560-4585); - Shavuos and the holy bird drawn out by whispering (4617-4625); - Rosh …

family: The Zohar, volume III: the One made whole below
title: Zohar, volume 3, part 11: Matot to Ha'Azinu (lines 4735-5313)
abstract: This is the Zohar on the Shema. Vaetchanan holds its fullest teaching on how to say "Hear O Israel" and "You shall love." It also covers: - how to go to sleep, rise at midnight, and stand in prayer (4743-4752); - the mezuzah as G-d standing guard at the door (4812-4859); - the Evil Urge as a guest who becomes the master of the house (4891-4893).

family: The Zohar, volume III: the One made whole below
title: Zohar, volume 3, part 12: the Idra Zuta in Ha'Azinu (lines 5314-5492)
abstract: The Idra Zuta ("the small gathering") is Rabbi Shimon's last day. The house fills. Fire surrounds it. Rabbi Hamnuna the Elder and seventy righteous souls come to listen, and so does the Holy One Himself (5314-5321). Rabbi Shimon says he wants to reveal what he held back in the great Idra, so that he will not "enter the world to come in shame" (line 5317). Rabbi Abba writes, Rabbi Elazar repeats, and the rest "whisper in their hearts" (line 5318).

family: The Zohar, volume III: the One made whole below
title: Zohar, volume 3, part 13: Addenda to volume III (lines 1-251)
abstract: The addenda are loose pieces, but several of them go straight to the inner life: - a hungry child, the son of Rav Hamnuna the Elder, teaches the order of offering (1-17); - Shabbos is a king's day with his bride and his children (18, 21); - the soul that speaks, and what bad speech does to it (28-32); - Torah scholars live on a small taste of the world to come (35-40); - a midnight prayer and a vision of G-d's delight in the righteous (78-98); - the serpent …

family: The Tikkunei Zohar and the Zohar Chadash
title: Zohar, part 4: the Tikkunei Zohar and the Zohar Chadash
abstract: The Tikkunei Zohar and the Zohar Chadash say the same thing about God from two sides. From His side: He is one, but not in number; He has no image, no measure and no partner; He is inside every world as He is outside it and does not change; there is no place empty of Him; and all before Him is as nothing.

family: The Tikkunei Zohar and the Zohar Chadash
title: Tikkunei Zohar, 1a-17b: the first introduction and Patach Eliyahu
abstract: The Tikkunei Zohar is seventy readings of one word, בראשית, "In the beginning", given by Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai in a cave while Elijah and the souls of the heavenly academy come down to listen. The book opens twice. The first introduction (1a-16b) teaches on the verse "the wise will shine like the brightness of the sky" and on the mitzvah of sending away the mother bird.

family: The Tikkunei Zohar and the Zohar Chadash
title: Tikkunei Zohar, 17b-42a: Tikkunim 1-20
abstract: After Patach Eliyahu the seventy tikkunim begin. Each takes the word בראשית apart a new way (ב' ראשית, "two beginnings"; ירא שבת, "fear Shabbat"; ברית אש, "covenant of fire"; שיר תאב, "a longed-for song") and finds in it a mitzvah or a secret. Tikkunim 1-20 run through the letter bet as the house of the King, the vowel points as the inner life of the letters, tefillin, Shabbat, sukkah and lulav, the order of the Amidah, prophecy, and the palaces of prayer.

family: The Tikkunei Zohar and the Zohar Chadash
title: Tikkunei Zohar, 42b-63a: Tikkun 21, the long tikkun of prayer, the heart and the Shechinah's names
abstract: Tikkun 21 is by far the longest tikkun, twenty folios. It is a book inside the book. Two old men and a mysterious boy (the son of Rav Hamnuna Saba, line 1424) meet Rabbi Shimon on the road. A herald cries that whoever kills the serpent will receive the King's daughter, who is prayer.

family: The Tikkunei Zohar and the Zohar Chadash
title: Tikkunei Zohar, 63b-111a: from the Sinai tikkun to "leit atar panui" and the doors of gilgul
abstract: The longest continuous run of the book: Elijah's praise of Rabbi Shimon's mouth as Sinai; the Ten Commandments as one word; the Shechinah's garments embroidered with every creature; "set me as a seal on your heart" read eight ways; the heart as a nut, a wine jug and a sick bride whose pulse only the Faithful Shepherd can read; Tikkun 30's cry "wake up, you sleepers"; the three kinds of fear; Ruth and Naomi as body and soul; the pardes of four rivers; Adam's sin and the two trees; Tikkun …

family: The Tikkunei Zohar and the Zohar Chadash
title: Tikkunei Zohar, 111a-148a: Cain's return, the face that shows the soul, and the Name in every limb
abstract: The last third of the book. Tikkun 69 ends on Cain: his offering of leftovers, his late teshuvah, and why God would still have taken him back. From there it turns to the breaths (hevel) of prayer, Moshe spread through every generation, and the most careful lines in the whole book on the Cause of causes who has no image and no partner. Tikkun 70 is the physiognomy tikkun.

family: The Tikkunei Zohar and the Zohar Chadash
title: Zohar Chadash, Bereshit: the one day, the one point, and a mind made to know its Master
abstract: The Zohar Chadash is the "new Zohar": pieces that did not make it into the printed three volumes, gathered in Safed and printed later. Its Bereshit section reads the six days of creation more than once. First it reads them as letters and points (the yud, the heh, the alef), then as the ten sefirot hidden in a nut, then, in the Midrash HaNe'elam, as a teaching on the soul and on how a person comes to know God.

family: The Tikkunei Zohar and the Zohar Chadash
title: Zohar Chadash, Eichah, Sifra Tanina, Tikuna Kadma'ah and the additions: the mother who left, one without number, and a gift in every limb
abstract: It begins with grief. The Midrash HaNe'elam on Eichah is a correspondence between the exiles in Babylon and those left in the Land of Israel, each saying they have more reason to weep; then God weeps, the patriarchs and Moshe rise from their graves, and Rachel will not be comforted. At midnight the Shechinah walks through the ruined Temple and speaks to her bed and her altar.

family: The Tikkunei Zohar and the Zohar Chadash
title: Zohar Chadash, Midrash Rut: tears that open every gate, the Name hidden in a person, and the table before the King
abstract: The Midrash on Ruth is the most human part of the Zohar Chadash. It reads the Book of Ruth twice over: once as the story of the soul (Naomi) and its parts (Ruth the intellectual soul, Orpah the animal soul, Elimelech the soul of the soul), and once as the Shechinah in exile. Around that it gathers many short stories. A sage hears a voice in the field on the mother bird and weeps for joy.

family: The Tikkunei Zohar and the Zohar Chadash
title: Zohar Chadash, Noach to Beshalach: the day examined, the open tunnel, and a God who waits
abstract: Seven short nodes on the Torah portions from Noach to Beshalach. The main thread is the soul: where it comes from, what it is for, how it is helped, and how it comes back when it strays. Noach turns into a long teaching on teshuvah and on speaking good of others. Lech Lecha reads Abraham's journey as the soul's descent into a body. Toldot has the wells Abraham and Isaac dug, read as the door to knowing God.

family: The Tikkunei Zohar and the Zohar Chadash
title: Zohar Chadash, Shir HaShirim: kisses to become one, David looking up in the wilderness, and the four knowings
abstract: Rabbi Shimon and his circle read the Song of Songs as the love of God and the Community of Israel, and, inside that, as the love of the soul for its source. The node reads "the song of songs" as a union of four radiances; "let him kiss me" as spirit joining spirit; "draw me after you" as running with desire.

family: The Tikkunei Zohar and the Zohar Chadash
title: Zohar Chadash, Terumah to Ki Tavo: prayer as giving the soul, the whispering heart, and the Measuring Line
abstract: Twelve nodes from Exodus to Deuteronomy. Terumah opens with the morning order of prayer read as a ladder, and the Mishkan as a dwelling below. Ki Tisa reads the Ten Commandments through thought, and makes fear the gate. Tzav has one short passage on turning a bad thought into a pure one. Achrei Mot has the Shema in the limbs, midnight, and a Shabbat home. Chukat reads Psalm 45 with the Song of Songs and David's "my heart whispers".

family: The Tikkunei Zohar and the Zohar Chadash
title: Zohar Chadash, Yitro: no place without Him, a mind that cannot hold Him, and the chariot seen in a whisper
abstract: Yitro is the second largest node in the Zohar Chadash and it has three parts. The first (to about line 1506) is a long physiognomy, like the Tikkunim's Tikkun 70: hair, forehead, eyes, nose and lips read as signs of a person's soul, with the constant note that teshuvah changes the signs. The second (about 1507 to 1530) is a passage on thought, speech and deed that reads like Patach Eliyahu and belongs with it; it is the unity core of the whole Zohar Chadash.

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
abstract: Ibn Gabbai wrote one idea three times, at twenty six, at fifty and at fifty eight: the service of G-d is a need on high (tzorech gavoah). The mitzvot and prayer are not only for us. They repair the Glory (the Kavod: the divine attributes as they turn toward the world) and unite it with the great Name. That is why the world was made, why the soul came down, and why man and not the angel is the purpose.

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Avodat HaKodesh, range 1: the introduction and the Part of Unity, chapters 1-12 (lines 1-139)
abstract: Avodat HaKodesh ("the holy service") has four parts: Unity (what G-d is and how the sefirot are one with Him), Service (what the service of man does above), Purpose (why man and the world exist), and the Secrets of the Torah. The introduction states the whole book in one idea, and this report gives it the most room because the rest of the work unfolds it: the soul came down as a stranger on earth to complete the will above; the service of man is a "need on high" (tzorech …

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Avodat HaKodesh, range 2: the Part of Unity, chapters 13-27 (lines 140-342)
abstract: The first chapters proved that the ten sefirot are G-d Himself. This range turns from the One to the one who serves Him. It asks why man was made in the image, why Israel, what the Torah is, what the mitzvot do, and then it names the two great doors of service: fear and love. Names and the one Name (140-163). "By My deeds I am called." Ehyeh three times: no change before, now or after. The four-letter Name holds all ten. How to say the Name.

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Avodat HaKodesh, range 3: the end of the Part of Unity and the Part of Service, chapters 1-14 (lines 343-553)
abstract: This is the range where the book's central teaching is argued in full. Part 2 opens: "I already wrote at the opening of this book that service is a need on high, not only a need of man" (line 362). Then fourteen chapters prove it, answer the objection that G-d needs nothing, and teach how to pray so that the prayer is wholly for Him.

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Avodat HaKodesh, range 4: the Part of Service, chapters 15-24 (lines 554-735)
abstract: The last range proved that service is a need on high. This range asks how it works, what comes of it, and why a soul was sent down to do it. How can the lower move the upper? (554-587). A rejected answer (two lutes tuned alike) and ibn Gabbai's own: man is built in the form of the upper Man, and the Torah is the thread that joins the two forms. The shadow that laughs when you laugh. Reward is the nature of the deed, not a promise (588-625).

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Avodat HaKodesh, range 5: the Part of Service, chapters 25-38 (lines 736-910)
abstract: The last range asked why the soul came down. This range follows the soul out of the body and back in, and then turns to return (teshuvah) and the end of days. The soul's garments and the Garden (736-793). The soul wears a fine garment in this world and another after it. The Garden of Eden is a real place below with a Garden above it. Who is alive and who is dead. Gehinnom (794-812). Free choice between two paths.

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Avodat HaKodesh, range 6: the end of Part 2 and the opening of the Part of Purpose (lines 911-1115)
abstract: This range holds the answer to the owner's main question: why was the world made? Ibn Gabbai gives it straight, against the Rambam. Why souls come back into bodies at the resurrection (911-930). The task was blocked by the evil inclination. When it is gone, body and soul will serve with nothing in the way. The world to come is body and soul (931-1014). Against the Rambam, who said souls only. As the service was in body and soul, so the reward.

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Avodat HaKodesh, range 7: the Part of Purpose, chapters 7-13 (lines 1116-1276)
abstract: Range 6 showed that man is the purpose of creation. This range asks what that means in practice. Why the angels opposed man (1116-1144). Because man can do what they cannot: unite G-d, not only praise Him. Israel's Shema is dearer than the angels' "Holy". Only G-d can make us righteous (1145-1160). We cannot know His will by our own reason. He gives it to us, and doing it makes us like Him. Man rules nature when he keeps his image (1161-1183).

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Avodat HaKodesh, range 8: the Part of Purpose, chapters 14-21 (lines 1277-1401)
abstract: Most of this range is a sharp attack on philosophy as a path to G-d. For the guide the attack matters less than what it protects: the claim that G-d's will and inner Torah are known by receiving, not by reasoning, and that a person reaches G-d by doing His will and being answered. Moses, the fullness of creation (1277-1291). Creation was "good" only when there was someone to receive the Torah. Reason cannot reach His will (1292-1305). Israel's wisdom is that they call and He answers.

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Avodat HaKodesh, range 9: the Part of Purpose, chapters 22-33 (lines 1402-1525)
abstract: The Torah comes from the upper Thought, and so does its explanation (1402-1410). The tablets were cut from "the place of full freedom". The voice that never stopped (1411-1426). If reasoning is forbidden, how can the sages argue and rule? Because the source still flows, and every true teaching was received at Sinai from "a great voice that did not stop". "These and these are the words of the living G-d." The Torah shows herself only to those who love her (1427-1436). The Zohar's maiden in the palace.

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Avodat HaKodesh, range 10: the Part of Purpose, chapters 34-47 (lines 1526-1653)
abstract: This range is ibn Gabbai's own answer to the Rambam's "Guide", word by word. The Rambam explained the Bible's human words for G-d ("see", "hear", "place", "throne", "sit", "stand", "rock") as figures of speech for created things or for G-d's actions. Ibn Gabbai explains each one as a name for unity: every "seeing" or "hearing" or "sitting" of G-d is the joining of His lights. And each is caused, in part, by us.

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Avodat HaKodesh, range 11: the end of the Part of Purpose, chapters 48-70 (lines 1654-1825)
abstract: More of the Bible's human words for G-d, read as unity (1654-1751). Near, full, high, pass, come, go out, walk, dwell, sad, eat, face, heart, spirit, soul, alive, wing. Each is a name for His joining of His lights, and each depends on us. Deed is the heart of it (1752-1787). The fruit of study is the mitzvah; the fruit of the mitzvah is the unity. A mitzvah is whole when it has act, knowledge and intention. Attributes (1788-1802).

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Avodat HaKodesh, range 12: the Part of Secrets, chapters 1-13 (lines 1826-1942)
abstract: Part 4 turns to the "Work of Creation" (maaseh bereishit) read as the story of the emanation above, with the lower creation as its mirror. Why write secrets at all (1826-1845). The inner wisdom was never lost, because it is a need on high. Ibn Gabbai, who says he knows only "a drop in the great sea", writes anyway: "the thing was in me like a burning fire". Why the world needed an in-between (1846-1848).

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Avodat HaKodesh, range 13: the Part of Secrets, chapters 14-24 (lines 1943-2088)
abstract: Cain, Abel and Seth (1943-1948). Good and evil come from one root, and the Messiah comes when evil turns to good. What unity means (1949-1953). The lower flame yearns for the upper one. The one who unites holds up the Presence in exile. Looking into the Chariot (1954-1963). Turning the heart from the world to the Chariot counts as praying all day. The patriarchs were the Chariot. Ezekiel's vision, verse by verse (1964-2023).

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Avodat HaKodesh, range 14: the Part of Secrets, chapters 25-36, and the close of the book (lines 2089-2224)
abstract: Why prophecy stopped (2089-2094). Baruch ben Neriah was ready, but the Temple and the generation were not. What prophecy is (2095-2128). Moses compared with the other prophets and with Balaam; vision and dream; prophecy comes from the unity itself, not from an angel. Angels and garments (2129-2141). Higher things reach lower ones only through a garment. Sinai (2142-2195). All souls stood there. The voice was not created. All Israel heard all ten words and became prophets in the whole Torah. The Exodus, above and below (2196-2202).

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Derekh Emunah (The Way of Faith): R. Meir ibn Gabbai on the sefirot (¶1-191)
abstract: A short book of answers. A student, Yosef HaLevi, wrote to ibn Gabbai with ten questions about the sefirot (the ten divine attributes through which G-d shows Himself) (¶3-18): How do we know the world has a Leader? Why must there be sefirot at all, and not only the Ein Sof (the Infinite)? Why ten, and how are they one power? Were they emanated or created? How can He be one while they are ten? Why do they have limit and measure? When did they come to be?

family: R. Meir ibn Gabbai: the service is a need on high
title: Tola'at Yaakov (The Worm of Jacob): R. Meir ibn Gabbai on the secrets of prayer
abstract: A book on the secrets of prayer and of the mitzvot of the day, "illuminating the prayers of the whole year in four ways: plain meaning, hint, homily and secret" (title page, p. 1). Ibn Gabbai finished it on 12 Nisan 5267 (spring 1507), and says at the end that he wrote it "while I was twenty six" (p. 95). It is his first book, written about a quarter century before Avodat HaKodesh, which names it (Avodat HaKodesh line 2200: the mitzvot are "a need on high ...

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
abstract: The Ramak is the great systematizer of Kabbalah before the Arizal, and the Chabad masters quote him by name. His unity has three parts. One simple Cause, beyond change. The Infinite is "the simple One, cause of all causes and reason of all reasons, removed from change and from attributes" (pardes-rimmonim line 353). He is one "not as one that is counted" (ohr-neerav line 432). All the changes we see, judgment and mercy, anger and favor, belong to His ten measures, the sefirot, and not to Him.

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Derishot BeInyanei HaMalachim (Inquiries on the Angels): the whole book
abstract: This is the Ramak's treatise on angels, in seven "inquiries": how many ranks there are, what they are, why they exist, their order, how a person receives from them, how a person "rides" them, and how a person can bind them to his will. Most of it is angelology: ranks, names, thrones, the Merkavah (the chariot vision). That part is not for the guide.

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Elima Rabbati: an OCR skim
abstract: Elima Rabbati is the Ramak's second great system after the Pardes. It is built as four "springs" (maayanot), each with "palm trees" (tamarim) of chapters: Ein Kol HaAretz (His existence, unity and providence), Ein HaBedolach (the Crown and emanation), Ein Ro'i, and Ein Shemesh (the chain of the sefirot).

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Ohr Ne'erav (The Pleasant Light): the whole book
abstract: Ohr Ne'erav is the Ramak's short door into the inner Torah. The Pardes is the house. This book stands at the gate and talks to three kinds of people who stay outside: those who say there is nothing inside, those who say it is too high for them, and those who are afraid of making a mistake.

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Or Yakar: on prophecy, and on Bereshit 1:1
abstract: Or Yakar (Precious Light) is the Ramak's huge commentary on the Zohar. Only two short portions were found in open typed form: a section on prophecy and a section on the first verse of Genesis. Both were read in full. The texts are typed copies from grimoar.cz, not checked against a printed edition.

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Pardes Rimmonim, lines 1-428: why there are sefirot at all
abstract: Pardes Rimmonim ("The Orchard of Pomegranates") is the Ramak's great system of Kabbalah, finished in 1548 when he was about 27. It has 32 gates. This range holds the front of the book and its first two gates. Gate 1 argues that the sefirot (the ten "measures" through which God acts) are exactly ten. Gate 2 asks why there is an emanation at all. Most of the pages are close reading of Sefer Yetzirah and the Zohar.

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Pardes Rimmonim, lines 429-581: the Infinite, the crown, and the light inside the vessels
abstract: These two gates are the heart of the Ramak's teaching on the unity of God. Gate 3 separates the Infinite (Ein Sof) from the first of the sefirot, the Crown (Keter), and says what sets the Infinite apart. Gate 4 asks the question that decides everything else: are the sefirot God Himself, or are they tools He uses?

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Pardes Rimmonim, lines 582-753: the order of the sefirot, and a world renewed every moment
abstract: Three technical gates: in what order the sefirot came out (Gate 5), how to picture them standing (Gate 6), and the "channels" by which one passes light to another (Gate 7). Most of the pages settle disputes among earlier Kabbalists. But inside them the Ramak says some of his strongest things about the unity: that every level is nested inside the one above it, all the way up to the Infinite, so that "one cannot say this is Malchut and not the Infinite"; that He brings all things into being …

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Pardes Rimmonim, lines 754-982: judgment as a hidden face, and the awakening from below
abstract: Gate 8, "Essence and Conduct" (Mahut veHanhagah), is the longest gate before the lexicon, and for the guide it may be the most useful. It asks what the sefirot are like as we meet them: which is mercy, which judgment, where judgment comes from, and how the upper world is moved.

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Pardes Rimmonim, lines 983-1225: wholeness of opposites, colors that move the soul, and the hidden lights
abstract: Four gates. Gate 9 asks who makes peace between Chesed (giving) and Gevurah (holding back), and answers that the whole one is the one who holds both. Gate 10 is about the colors of the sefirot: they are not real colors, yet a color seen by the eye or pictured in the mind can wake the soul.

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Pardes Rimmonim, lines 1226-1455: fifty gates, returning light, and the King in weekday clothes
abstract: Four gates that turn the Ramak's map toward time and toward the world we live in. Gate 13 counts the fifty gates of Binah (understanding) through the fifty times the Torah says "I brought you out of Egypt", and from there reads time itself: hours, days, weeks, years, each a channel from the one above; Egypt as a furnace for gathering lost sparks; the counting of the Omer as a daily practice. Gate 14 says the spiritual never loses its earlier form when it unfolds.

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Pardes Rimmonim, lines 1456-1630: the moon made small, and the Names as handles
abstract: Four gates. Gate 17 reads the Zohar on the angel who struck Jacob's thigh, and uses it to say something the guide needs: the shells never enter the divine world; their "entry" is only an accusation that makes mercy turn its face. Gate 18 is the Talmud's story of the moon who said "two kings cannot share one crown" and was told "go, make yourself small". The Ramak works through three readings and a hard question: how can there be complaint inside holiness?

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Pardes Rimmonim, lines 1631-1801: the detailed Names, and a person as a chariot
abstract: Two gates. Gate 21 is the densest in the book: the long "particular Names" of God (the 72-triplet Name from Exodus 14, the 42-letter Name from Genesis 1, the 22-letter Name from the priestly blessing, the 12 diagonal boundaries, the 54 and 72 permutations). Most of it is tables. But it opens with a full quotation of an Abulafian meditation on the Name (from "Sefer HaNikud"), and it is full of guards on what may and may not be done with Names.

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Pardes Rimmonim, lines 1802-2380: the lexicon of names, alef to kaf
abstract: Gate 23 is a dictionary: every word the Zohar and the Tikkunim use for a sefirah, in the order of the alef-bet, with what it means and where. It is the longest gate and the one later kabbalists used most. Much of it is technical ("which sefirah is 'arm', which is 'thigh'").

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Pardes Rimmonim, lines 2381-2962: the lexicon of names, kaf to tav
abstract: This is the second half of Gate 23, the dictionary of God's names, from kaf to tav. Most entries are short and technical. But in the second half the Ramak keeps stopping to teach, and some of his clearest lines on the unity and on the inner life sit here. He writes about speech as the pattern for how anything comes to be. He calls Binah a question with no answer.

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Pardes Rimmonim, lines 2963-3106: palaces, angels, and the shells
abstract: These three gates move from God's own levels down to the worlds below them. Gate 24 describes the seven palaces of holiness, with their angels and gates. Gate 25 asks where evil comes from and why it exists. Gate 26 describes the seven palaces of the "other side". The Ramak says plainly that most of this is copied, not his own. The palaces carry "no new matter from the side of contemplation at all" (ואין בענין ההיכלות האלו ענין מחודש מחלק העיון כלל, line 2964).

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Pardes Rimmonim, lines 3107-3270: letters, vowels, and cantillation
abstract: These three gates are about the stuff that holy speech is made of. Gate 27 covers the twenty-two letters, Gate 28 the vowel points, and Gate 29 the cantillation marks. Most of the letter-by-letter and vowel-by-vowel pages are technical. They say which letter hints at which sefirah, and what Sefer HaTemunah and Brit Menuchah say about each shape. That material and the names of the "lights" of each vowel are not for the guide.

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Pardes Rimmonim, lines 3271-3445: combination, the soul, and intention
abstract: These are the last three gates of the Pardes. Gate 30 lays out the tables of letter-combination, substitution and gematria. It is technical, and its one practical passage, name-permutation in seclusion, is not for the guide. The Ramak himself hedges it (line 3277). Gates 31 and 32 are the book's landing place, where all the maps come back to the person.

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Sefer Gerushin (The Book of Wanderings): the whole book
abstract: In the winter of 1548 the Ramak, his teacher and brother-in-law R. Shlomo Alkabetz, and a few friends began to go out of Safed on foot. They walked to ruined study houses, caves and the graves of the sages of the Mishnah. On the way they opened a verse, with no book and no preparation, and spoke what came. They called these walks gerushin (wanderings, or exiles), because they went out into exile together with the Shechinah (the Presence of God in the world, who is also in exile).

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: The Ramak on Sefer Yetzirah: the whole commentary
abstract: Sefer Yetzirah (the Book of Formation) is the oldest book of Jewish mysticism: 32 paths of wisdom, ten sefirot and twenty-two letters by which God made the world. The Ramak wrote a commentary on it as "gates" 14 to 19 of a larger work. Most of it explains the sefirot and the letters. Chapter 2 is long tables of letter-pairs (lines 231-331), which are technical and not for the guide.

family: The Ramak: one Cause, ten garments, and a person who walks like his Maker
title: Tomer Devorah (The Palm Tree of Devorah): the whole book
abstract: Tomer Devorah is the Ramak's small book of how to live. The Pardes maps God's ten sefirot. Tomer Devorah turns each one into a way of treating people, starting with the thirteen attributes of mercy (Micah 7:18-20). Its first sentence is the whole program: "a person should make himself like his Maker" (האדם ראוי שיתדמה לקונו, line 1).

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: The Maharal: the One who is not a number, a world that is one because He is One, and a person who cleaves
abstract: The Maharal is the great thinker of oneness before the Ari's teachings spread. He almost never uses Kabbalistic terms. He argues from the nature of the one and the many, the simple and the made-up, the cause and what it causes. His whole teaching comes down to four sentences. He is simple, so nothing stands outside Him.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Be'er HaGolah, lines 1-250: Oneness From Every Side, and the G-d Who Prays
abstract: Be'er HaGolah (The Well of the Exile) defends the words of the sages against seven complaints. Each "well" answers one complaint. This first half covers the Introduction, Wells 1-3 (rabbinic laws, laws that look strange, and readings of verses that look forced), and the first part of Well 4 (aggadot that seem to say strange things about G-d). Knowing your lack is a level. "Living flesh feels the scalpel, and dead flesh does not" (11). To feel what you lack is already a sign of life. Oneness cancels harm.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Be'er HaGolah, lines 251-529: His Will Joins, the Middle Point, and the Key of the Receiver
abstract: The second half of Be'er HaGolah finishes the aggadot about G-d (Well 4), then defends sayings that look like tall tales (Well 5), sayings that seem to clash with science (Well 6), and laws and prayers that seem harsh to outsiders (Well 7). Again and again the Maharal says the sages speak of the essence of a thing, not its bodily size, and that every "change" in G-d is on the side of the receiver.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Derashat Shabbat HaGadol, lines 1-271: Nothing But Him, the Name That Is 'What', and Walking Toward Peace
abstract: This is the Maharal's sermon for the Shabbat before Pesach (1589). It opens with "G-d made all for His sake", explains the Pesach offering as service to the One, then reads the offerings of Parashat Tzav (olah, mincha, chatat, todah, shelamim) as a map of a person's inner life: pride and lowness, the evil inclination, thanks, and peace. "There is none else" means nothing else. Not only no other god: "there is nothing else in the world but G-d" (2).

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Derekh Chayyim, lines 1-419: Nothing but G-d and What Is From Him, Love and Awe From One Root, and Joining All Until All Is One
abstract: Derekh Chayyim ("The Way of Life") is the Maharal's commentary on Pirkei Avot (Ethics of the Fathers). This range covers his introduction, the opening mishna, and the first two chapters. The book is about musar (the training of character). But the Maharal grounds every rule of character in one claim about G-d: nothing stands by itself, and all being is from Him.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Derekh Chayyim, lines 420-717: The Evil Inclination as Twoness, the Caused Cleaving to the Cause, and the One Who Is All
abstract: This is chapter 3 of Pirkei Avot in the Maharal's commentary. It opens with "look at three things and you will not come to sin" and closes with the straight road of halacha (Jewish law). In between is some of the Maharal's clearest teaching on how the One relates to the many. The evil inclination is twoness. "שהיצר הוא השניות" (428): "for the inclination is twoness." From G-d's side, who is One, it should not exist. So the Shema (the declaration that G-d is One) drives it away.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Derekh Chayyim, lines 718-1060: The Name as Essence, Only the One Judges Alone, and Moving Toward Him Is Being With Him
abstract: This is chapter 4 of Pirkei Avot in the Maharal's commentary. It holds Ben Zoma's "who is wise, strong, rich, honored," the call to be "very, very lowly of spirit," the three crowns and the crown of a good name, "this world is a corridor," and the last mishna: "those born are to die, and the dead to live." None judges alone but the One. A person must not judge alone, "because He is One, apart from all beings, and has no partner" (831).

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Derekh Chayyim, lines 1061-1696: One From the Maker's Side, the Maharal Against the Rambam on Knowing, the One Who Unites Opposites, and the Torah of the Forty-Eight Ways
abstract: This is the last part of Derekh Chayyim: chapter 5 of Pirkei Avot ("with ten sayings the world was made") and chapter 6, the added chapter on acquiring Torah. It holds the Maharal's longest direct argument about G-d's attributes, aimed at the Rambam and the philosophers. It also holds his teaching on "a dispute for the sake of Heaven," where G-d is the One who unites opposites.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Derush al HaTorah, lines 1-257: Be a Desert, Be One, and Want It First
abstract: Derush al HaTorah (A Sermon on the Torah) was given for Shavuot. It reads the verses before Sinai ("In the third month... they came to the desert of Sinai") one by one, and asks: what makes a person able to receive the Torah? The last third is a sharp call to fix how Torah was being learned in his day: review, learn Mishnah first, learn every day, and stop empty sharpness.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Drashot Maharal, lines 59-141: Learning That Becomes Deed, the Four Letters of the Name, and Cleaving With No Barrier
abstract: The Sefaria file "Drashot Maharal" holds four sermons. Lines 1-58 are the introduction and the sermon on the Torah. They are the same text as Derush al HaTorah, with small spelling changes. I read two chunks of them in full and compared the rest by machine against derush-al-hatorah.txt. That report covers them, so they are not repeated here. Line 141 is only a note that the Shabbat HaGadol sermon has moved to a new edition. That sermon has its own report (derashat-shabbat-hagadol-1-271.md).

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Gevurot Hashem, lines 1-443: the simple One, faith as strength, the inner fruit in the outer peel
abstract: Gevurot Hashem ("The Mighty Acts of G-d") is the Maharal's book on the Exodus and the Pesach night. It was printed in Krakow in 1582. It opens with three long introductions about miracles and nature. Then it walks through the story from Avraham to the sea, and it ends with the seder and the Haggadah. This first range holds the introductions and the chapters up to Moshe as a young man.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Gevurot Hashem, lines 444-982: the bush, the Name, the plagues, the sea, the three bonds
abstract: This range carries the Exodus story from Moshe at the well of Midian to the splitting of the sea, then turns to the mitzvot that came out of it (tefillin, the first-born, the festivals). It is the richest part of the book for the unity of G-d. Here the Maharal explains the burning bush, the Names Ehyeh and Havayah (the four-letter Name), why the One can bring both a wound and its healing, why harmful forces have no hold on oneness, and why awe comes from His separateness while love …

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Gevurot Hashem, lines 983-1863: the Song, the Haggadah, and the return of all things to their Cause
abstract: The last part of the book. Chapter 47 reads the Song at the Sea. Chapters 48-50 are the laws of the seder night. From chapter 51 the Maharal reads the Haggadah line by line, then Hallel. Chapters 66-72 step back and ask what the whole Exodus was for. The answer: so that G-d would dwell below, and so that all things would return to their Cause. The book closes with a short summary of the Pesach laws and a sharp halakhic tract against drinking non-Jewish wine.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Gur Aryeh on Bamidbar, lines 1-440: The One That Is Not a Number, the Torah as the Middle That Joins, Every Act Needs a Doer Below, and No Quarrel Beyond the Line
abstract: This is the first half of the Maharal's commentary on Rashi's Bamidbar: the census and the camps, the levites, the nazir, the priestly blessing, the gifts of the princes, the menorah, the cloud, the complainers, the spies, the libations and challah, tzitzit, and Korach. Much is law, and the sotah and other passages are left out under D28. But this half holds some of the Maharal's clearest words on how a person is joined to G-d.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Gur Aryeh on Bamidbar, lines 441-804: Oneness Is Kingship, Faith Is Joy, Look Up and Bind the Heart, and Cleave to the One Who Renews the Light
abstract: This is the second half of the Maharal's commentary on Rashi's Bamidbar: the red cow, the death of Miriam, the waters of strife, the death of Aharon, the copper snake, Sichon and Og, Balak and Bilam, Pinchas, the new census, the daughters of Tzelofchad, the daily and holiday offerings, vows, the war on Midian, the journeys, and the cities of refuge. Much is law, war, or about nations and women, and is left out under D28.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Gur Aryeh on Bereishit, lines 1-707: One Day With No Twoness, Words That Name His Acts, the Screen Lifted, and Man Who Makes All One
abstract: Gur Aryeh is the Maharal's commentary on Rashi. Most of it is close work on words: why Rashi said this, why the verse wrote that. Many lines are grammar or law. But every few pages the Maharal stops and opens a large idea in a few lines. This report gathers those lines from the first half of Bereishit, from creation to Avraham's servant going to find a wife for Yitzchak.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Gur Aryeh on Bereishit, lines 708-1416: Only One in the Heart, the Place of the World, Being Is Good, and the Father Who Did Not Die
abstract: This is the second half of the Maharal's commentary on Rashi's Bereishit: Yitzchak and Rivka, Yaakov and Esav, the ladder, Lavan, the return, Yosef and his brothers, the descent to Egypt, and Yaakov's blessings and death. As in the first half, most lines are close reading of Rashi. But the Yaakov lines hold some of the Maharal's deepest words on oneness.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Gur Aryeh on Devarim, lines 1-294: He Is All and Nothing Is Outside Him, the Voice That Does Not Stop, One Now and One in the End, and Love That Makes Two Into One
abstract: This is the first half of the Maharal's commentary on Rashi's Devarim: Moshe's rebuke in hints, the judges, the spies recalled, the journeys past Edom and Moav, Moshe's prayer to enter the Land, the Ten Commandments again, the Shema and its second part, the laws of the chosen place, and "you are children to Hashem." Some passages about nations and women are left out under D28. The unity teaching in this half is among the richest in all of Gur Aryeh.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Gur Aryeh on Devarim, lines 295-653: One Power With None Beside It, Kingship Is Oneness, He Returns With Us From Exile, and the Level With No Division
abstract: This is the last part of Gur Aryeh: the laws of food and tithes, the festivals, judges and kings, prophets, witnesses, war, the laws between people, bikkurim, the curses, Nitzavim, the song of Haazinu, Moshe's blessings, and his death. A large part is law, war, and passages on nations, women and unions, all left out under D28. What remains closes the whole work with its clearest words on oneness.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Gur Aryeh on Shemot, lines 1-470: Ehyeh and Havaya, the Name Above Time, His Care for Each Detail, and the Radiance of the Shechina
abstract: This is the first half of the Maharal's commentary on Rashi's Shemot: the slavery, the burning bush, the plagues, Pesach, the sea, the manna, Amalek, and Yitro's coming. Most lines are close reading of Rashi. But some of the Maharal's clearest words on the Names of G-d are here. He explains what each Name tells us, and what no Name can tell.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Gur Aryeh on Shemot, lines 471-968: The Torah as One Word, Glory Spreading in All, Mercy That Does Not Change, and the Act Below
abstract: This is the second half of the Maharal's commentary on Rashi's Shemot: the judges, Sinai and the Ten Commandments, the laws, the Mishkan and the priests' garments, the golden calf, Moshe's prayers, the Thirteen Attributes, and the building of the Mishkan. Much of it is law. But three of the Maharal's great teachings on oneness are here: the Torah is one word, true glory spreads into all beings, and He does not change even after sin.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Gur Aryeh on Vayikra, lines 1-460: Called by Name, the Low Near the High, Moshe the Simple, and the Menorah From the World of Oneness
abstract: This is the first half of the Maharal's commentary on Rashi's Vayikra: the offerings, the eight days of the Mishkan's start, the death of Nadav and Avihu, the laws of kosher and impure animals, and the laws of skin disease. It is the most legal part of Gur Aryeh so far. Most lines weigh one reading of a verse against another. But a few lines open onto the Maharal's larger thought.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Gur Aryeh on Vayikra, lines 461-873: The Blessing That Gives the Earth, Holiness as Setting Apart, Everything Returns to Its First Standing, and He Is Joined to Us in Exile
abstract: This is the second half of the Maharal's commentary on Rashi's Vayikra: Yom Kippur, the forbidden foods and unions, Kedoshim, the laws of the kohanim, the festivals, the menorah and the showbread, shemitah and yovel, the blessings and the curses, and the vows of value. Much is law, and a large part is left out under D28. But some of the Maharal's most useful teachings for daily life are here.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Ner Mitzvah, lines 1-90: The One and the Four Sides, and the Candle of the Soul
abstract: Ner Mitzvah (The Candle of the Mitzvah) is a short book for Chanukah. Volume I explains why there are four kingdoms that rule the world before the end. Volume II explains the Chanukah miracle and some laws of the lights, and ends with a sharp call to keep the community's fences. Most of Volume I compares peoples and kingdoms. For the guide only its frame is used: why a world made by the One has lack in it, and how the One relates to the "four sides".

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Netivot Olam, lines 1-411: the Introduction and the Path of Torah
abstract: Lines 330-351 hold very harsh words about the ignorant (am haaretz). They are not used below. Even there the Maharal adds that no one may be written off, since "at any moment he may become a sage" (351).

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Netivot Olam, lines 412-636: the Paths of Service, Chesed, Tzedakah, Judgment and Truth
abstract: This range is the Maharal's handbook of prayer and of giving. The Path of Service (Avodah) walks through the day: waking, the Shema, the Amidah, bowing, Amen, blessings over food, grace after meals, and the Shema at bedtime. Then come the paths of chesed (lovingkindness), tzedakah (charity), judgment and truth. It is the richest range in the book for practice.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Netivot Olam, lines 637-815: Faith, Peace, Love of a Fellow, Humility, Awe of G-d, and the Tongue
abstract: Lines 796-811 are letters and bans from the Maharal's time against people who called certain families mamzerim. They are history, not teaching, and are not used below. Some lines on the nations (698) and on women and slaves (766) are also set aside under D28.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Netivot Olam, lines 816-930: Love of G-d, Silence, Holiness, Modesty, the Evil Inclination, and the Righteous
abstract: This range opens with the Path of Love of G-d, which contains the Maharal's most direct words on the unity of G-d in the whole book: love of G-d is possible because He is One and there is nothing besides Him, so all returns to Him.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Netivot Olam, lines 931-1248: Returning through Decent Conduct
abstract: Left out of this report under D28: the harsh words on nations in the Shame path (1156), and the ranking of women and slaves as witnesses in Derech Eretz (1242). The bitter lament over his own community (1150) is history and is not used.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Netzach Yisrael, lines 1-450: Exile, the One and the Many, the Bond That Cannot Break
abstract: Netzach Yisrael ("The Eternity of Israel") is the Maharal's book on exile and redemption. It asks a hard question. If a people is bound to G-d, why does it suffer so long? The first half, covered here, is mostly about exile: why it came, why it lasts, and why it cannot be forever. For our purposes the book matters because of what it says on the way.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Netzach Yisrael, lines 451-970: Ruin as the Start of Being, and 'His Name Will Be One'
abstract: The second half of Netzach Yisrael turns from exile to redemption. It asks what the "end" is, why it is hidden, what changes when it comes, and what kind of bond with G-d will then be complete. Absence comes before being. Nothing new comes to be unless the old has first fully passed. So ruin can be the first step of a higher being. He is One in Himself always; what changes is the receiver.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Ohr Chadash, lines 1-427: The Hidden Miracle, Knowing I Lack, the Water Channel From the One, and the Door Left Open Upward
abstract: Ohr Chadash ("New Light") is the Maharal's commentary on Megillat Esther. It asks why a book with no open miracle and no written Name of G-d is still a book of His hand. This first half covers the long introduction and the first two chapters: the king's feast, Vashti, and the rise of Mordechai and Esther. The miracle was hidden because it was so great.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Ohr Chadash, lines 428-990: The Heart in One's Power, Nature as His Messenger, Straightness With No End, and Standing as Nothing
abstract: This is the second half of the Maharal's commentary on Megillat Esther: Haman's rise, the decree, Mordechai in sackcloth, Esther's fast and her going to the king, the sleepless night, Haman's fall, the second letters, and the setting of Purim. Most of it reads the story line by line. The deep lines are few, but some are among the Maharal's best.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Tiferet Yisrael, lines 1-520: The Torah That Joins, and 'He Is Found as the Receiver Can Take Him'
abstract: Tiferet Yisrael ("the Glory of Israel") is the Maharal's book on the Torah: what it is, why it was given, how it joins a person to G-d, and how the giving at Sinai happened. The first half runs from the Introduction to the start of his long reading of the Ten Commandments. The Torah joins a person to G-d on every side. A good trait joins you to G-d in one way only. The Torah, taken as a whole, joins you fully.

family: The Maharal: the One who is not a number
title: Tiferet Yisrael, lines 521-1042: 'Anochi' Is His Very Self, and Faith Is the Cleaving
abstract: The second half of Tiferet Yisrael reads the Ten Commandments word by word, then turns to the lasting of the Torah: why it cannot change, why it seems forgotten, why the world to come is not written in it, how mitzvot are paid, and why the Torah is split into written and oral. It ends with "the four cubits of halacha" and the offering as the return of the caused to its Cause.

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment, and a day built to live it
abstract: The Shelah is the great bridge between Safed and the Chassidic masters. He gathers the Zohar, the Ramak, the early Ari circle, the Reshit Chochmah and the Chovot HaLevavot into one book of practice, and the Chassidic masters read him daily. His unity has three parts. There is no existence but His. "There is no other reality in the world but His reality, for if He hid it, all would be lost" (line 3938).

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Asara Hillulim and Vavei HaAmudim (lines 10782-10925): a daily ten-gate summary of the duties of the heart, and his son's six pillars; He brings all into being and gives all life always; truth is His seal because He is One
abstract: This last range holds two works. The first, Asara Hillulim ("Ten Praises"), is the Shelah's short summary of the Chovot HaLevavot (Duties of the Heart) in ten gates. He asks that one gate be read every day, "in heart and tongue", and then started again, forever (line 10783). It is the most practical page in the whole book.

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Asara Maamarot (lines 836-1296): the ladder of service
abstract: "The Ten Utterances" is the first of the three parts the Shelah promised in Toldot Adam. Where Toldot Adam built the theory (man in the image, the Torah as the Name, service as a need on high), this part is a ladder of the inner life. He lists ten "utterances", "all included in one utterance: He is the true One" (line 838), and then climbs them:

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Aseret HaDibrot, Pesachim (lines 3355-4263): kindness, renewal every moment, the inner search, the story that joins
abstract: Pesach is the pillar of kindness (chesed); "Pesach" means "He had pity" (line 3356). The tractate holds the laws of Rosh Chodesh, Pesach and the Omer; a long section on kindness (weddings, the sick, the dying, guests); six sermons for Shabbat HaGadol that the Shelah calls Matzah Ashirah ("rich matzah"); his Haggadah commentary Matzah Shemurah ("guarded matzah"); and a short ethics chapter. The sermons are among the richest pages in the book on the unity of G-d.

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Aseret HaDibrot, Rosh HaShanah and Yoma (lines 4960-5802): return as grace, seclusion with G-d, against needless self-affliction, the heart as His dwelling
abstract: Rosh HaShanah is the pillar of judgment (din); Yoma is the pillar of return (teshuvah). Together this is the book's manual of return. Much of it is quoted: from the Shelah's father's Emek Beracha and Brit Avraham, from Rabbeinu Yonah, the Rambam, Reishit Chochmah, Sefer Charedim, the Ramak and the Ari's circle. The Shelah weaves them and adds his own rulings. Two findings matter most for the guide.

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Aseret HaDibrot, Shevuot and Taanit (lines 4264-4959): the Torah as His oneness, nothing but His existence, study that acts, the broken heart as offering
abstract: Shevuot is the pillar of Torah. The Shelah gives the laws of the festival night and a long code of how to learn; then a great essay on Psalm 19 ("the Torah of G-d is whole"), in six steps: the Giver, the Torah, those who learn it, those who do it, Moshe the go-between, and "these and these are words of the living G-d".

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Aseret HaDibrot, Sukkah, Tamid and Megillah (lines 5803-6169): joy of body and soul for His Name, peace as unity of souls, the Shelah's manual of prayer, the three levels of the attributes, joy with the poor
abstract: This range closes the Aseret HaDibrot part of the book. Sukkah is the pillar of peace. Tamid (the daily offering) holds the Shelah's longest teaching on prayer. Megillah joins Purim to charity. Three findings matter most for the guide. First, the middle way of body and soul: the Creator joined a high soul to a dark body "so that both would live together", and a joy aimed at His Name turns even food and drink into service.

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Aseret HaDibrot: introduction, Chullin, Shabbat (lines 2668-3354): holy weekdays, the one day, rest of the heart
abstract: Here the Shelah opens his second great book, the "Ten Utterances" (Aseret HaDibrot). He builds it on ten pillars (line 2668): Torah, service, kindness, justice, truth, peace, return, prayer, charity, and faith, which holds them all. Each pillar gets a season and a tractate. Weekdays (Chullin, "ordinary things") are the pillar of truth; Shabbat is the pillar of faith. Each tractate has three chapters: Ner Mitzvah (the law), Torah Ohr (the inner reasons), and Derech Chayim (the path, ethics).

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Kedushat HaAchilah (lines 1727-2325): the table as altar
abstract: "The holiness of eating" closes the letter kuf (holiness). It is long and mostly law: forbidden foods and the Shelah's own stricter rulings (lines 1732-1818), the laws of the Land of Israel (1819-1871), health and danger (1872-1888), and a whole code of the blessings on food taken from his father's Emek Beracha (2113-2325). Inside the law sits a strong teaching: eating is where the body and the soul are joined, and a table can be an altar.

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Shaar HaOtiyot (lines 1297-1726): the alphabet of traits
abstract: "The Gate of Letters" is the Shelah's book of traits, one trait for each letter of the alphabet (line 1297). It is his most practical part: how to get up, how to do business, how to treat a wife, a child, an enemy, a stranger, one's own body. The unity of G-d stands under it all, and in a few places he says so outright.

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Shaar HaOtiyot end (lines 2326-2667): holy union, good will, silence, longing
abstract: The last pages of the Gate of Letters close the letter kuf (holiness) and then give the last three letters: resh for ratzon (good will, being easy to please), shin for shetikah (silence), tav for teshukah (longing). The Shelah ends by joining the three into one word, shevach, praise: silence, the nightly check, and desire.

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Toldot Adam (lines 1-835): the unity, the states and the practice
abstract: Toldot Adam ("The Generations of Man") is the long opening of the Shelah. R. Yeshayahu Horowitz wrote it as the door to the whole book, an ethical will to his children made as he left Prague for the Land of Israel (line 23). He says why he opens with it: to show "how awesome man is", so that a reader who sees that his hand "rules over everything and makes an impression" above will burn to cleave to G-d (line 37).

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebe'al Peh (lines 10293-10781): the whole Torah is His Names; the plain sense is above and ours is its garment; these and these are the words of the living G-d; learn in pairs, aloud, with joy, and ask for help
abstract: This part is a handbook of Talmud method. The Shelah wrote it in Jerusalem (line 10293). It is built on 27 "rules", one for each letter of "for by these words I made a covenant with you" (line 10294). Most of it is technical. It covers the thirteen rules of interpretation, the ways of the Mishnah, the Tosefta and the baraitot, and the terms of the Talmud from aleph to tav. It gives the rules for deciding the law and the lineage of the sages. It was all read.

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Chukat through V'Zot HaBerachah (lines 9407-10292): He is all, one without division; the more you grasp, the more you grasp that He cannot be grasped; hidden in essence, revealed in deeds; cling in every act; humility is the root of all traits; praise and blame equal
abstract: This range closes the Shelah's commentary on the Written Torah. It has the book's plainest statements of the unity. The Zohar's "He is all; He alone is all; He is one without division" (line 10242). "There is none but Him" (line 9695). Idolatry defined as a thought "that there is any divinity or power in the world besides Him" (line 9593). And the rule for how He is known: "whoever grasps most grasps most that He cannot be grasped" (line 9700).

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Introduction through Vayetzei (lines 6170-7002): the world as His guests every moment, He is the place of the world, awakening from below, readiness counts as the deed, the reward of a mitzvah is the mitzvah
abstract: Here the book turns to the weekly Torah portions. For each portion the Shelah gives the mitzvah it holds (Ner Mitzvah), its reasons and secrets (Torah Ohr), and the traits and practices it teaches (Derech Chayim). This range covers the introduction and the first seven portions of Genesis.

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Mishpatim through Pekudei (lines 7832-8455): He contracted Himself to bring limit into being; He sees and is not seen; the Essence Name is not grasped; souls a part of G-d above; what is below is dearer than what is above; a small Shabbat every day
abstract: This range covers the laws of Mishpatim and the building of the Mishkan (the desert sanctuary). It is one of the richest stretches of the book for the unity. Three things stand out. First, the Shelah's own statement of tzimtzum: the Endless, "by His great power without limit, brought limit into being", "contracted Himself" for this, and "is within them and surrounds them without end" (line 8095).

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Vayikra through Korach (lines 8456-9406): nothing exists apart from Him; He longed for a dwelling below; the Cause of all causes is the true general that holds all; the offering is yourself; a small Shabbat every day; the gates of return are always open; guard the edge
abstract: The Shelah reads all of Leviticus as one work: Torat Kohanim is "the repair of man". Before the first sin "all times were equal in holiness", and man "himself was an offering to G-d" (line 8457). Everything after, the offerings, the priests, the laws of purity, is a way back. The unity lines of this range come mostly out of that theme. "There is no existence at all that is apart from Him" (line 8709). He "longed to have a dwelling in the lower worlds" (line 8779).

family: The Shelah: nothing but His existence, renewed each moment
title: Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Torah Shebikhtav, Vayishlach through Yitro (lines 7003-7831): know it in the heart, not only by tradition; if He withheld for a moment they would be as nothing; before the will only necessary being, and that by negation; the higher, the more one; all Israel one soul
abstract: This range runs from Jacob's meeting with Esau to the giving of the Torah. Two passages carry most of the weight for the unity. In Vaera the Shelah says we were commanded to know that G-d is the only power, "with true knowledge", and that faith from tradition "is not enough" (line 7491). He adds that if G-d held back His power "for one moment", every force in the world "would be as if it had never been" (line 7506).

family: The Piaseczner Rebbe: the inner meditative world
title: The Piaseczner Rebbe: the inner meditative world
abstract: The Piaseczner Rebbe is the Chassidic master who wrote most plainly about what meditation is like from the inside. His whole method rests on one claim: the soul is already there, already moved, already singing and crying toward God, and we simply do not hear it. So the work is not to manufacture a feeling.

family: The Piaseczner Rebbe: the inner meditative world
title: Bnei Machshava Tova: the inner meditative world
abstract: The file is 339 lines. The text is unvocalised Sefaria-style Hebrew, with some Yiddish.

family: The Piaseczner Rebbe: the inner meditative world
title: Chovat HaTalmidim: the inner meditative world
abstract: Introduction, "A talk with teachers and fathers" (lines 1-48). "Chanoch la-na'ar al pi darko" means uncovering and growing the potential already hidden in the child. It does not mean command and habit. The Rebbe diagnoses his generation: the child's ego and feelings mature early and are unripe. So feeling has to be won for holiness from childhood, and dry intellect is not enough. This is where he states the founding principle: start with low, bodily arousal and let it wake the soul (lines 36-39, from the Pardes).

family: The Piaseczner Rebbe: the inner meditative world
title: Derekh HaMelekh, file lines 337-683: the inner meditative world
abstract: Source: Chassidus-txt/R. Kalonymus Kalman Shapira of Piaseczno (1889-1943)/Derekh HaMelekh (Warsaw, 1931).txt, lines 337-683. Every Hebrew line quoted below was checked with find_he.py verify ... --line N and came back FOUND at the line given. These are Sabbath talks (derashot) from 5685-5698 (1925-1938), weekly Torah portions from Vayigash to Balak. They are homilies, not a manual, but almost every one ends in "our work" (עבודתנו), and several hold the most concrete instructions for inner practice in the book.

family: The Piaseczner Rebbe: the inner meditative world
title: Derekh HaMelekh, file lines 684-982: the inner meditative world
abstract: Source: Chassidus-txt/R. Kalonymus Kalman Shapira of Piaseczno (1889-1943)/Derekh HaMelekh (Warsaw, 1931).txt, lines 684-982. This range covers the last of the Torah-portion talks (Balak to Ha'azinu, several from 5696/1936) and then Part II, the festival talks: nine Rosh Hashanah talks (5686-5691), three for Shabbat Shuvah, one on the Thirteen Attributes, and the opening of Motzaei Yom Kippur 5686.
