family: The Piaseczner Rebbe: the inner meditative world
title: Derekh HaMelekh, lines 1-336: the inner meditative world
abstract: Derekh HaMelekh ("The King's Way") collects the Shabbos and festival talks the Piaseczner Rebbe gave in Piaseczno and Warsaw between about 1928 and 1933. The file is labelled "Warsaw, 1931", but this range already includes talks dated תרצ"א and תרצ"ג, so the file follows a later, expanded edition. Unlike Bnei Machshava Tova, this is not a manual. These are sermons on the weekly portion.

family: The Piaseczner Rebbe: the inner meditative world
title: Derekh HaMelekh, lines 1309-1620: the inner meditative world
abstract: Every Hebrew line below was checked with find_he.py verify and came back FOUND at the line given. English renderings are mine. "L." means the file line.

family: The Piaseczner Rebbe: the inner meditative world
title: Esh Kodesh: the inner meditative world
abstract: Front matter (lines 1-56). Title page, the 1960 editors' account of finding the manuscript in Warsaw, and the Rebbe's Yiddish and Hebrew notice asking the finder to send his writings to his brother in Tel Aviv. Then his letter of 26 Tevet 5703 (January 1943) asking that his books be printed and studied, and memorial dedications to his mother, wife, son, daughter-in-law, and to his daughter Rechil Yehudis, "snatched from me" in Elul 1942 (line 42).

family: The Piaseczner Rebbe: the inner meditative world
title: Hakhsharat HaAvrekhim: the inner practice
abstract: Line numbers are lines of the source file. Chapter and paragraph references (e.g. 4:12) follow the file's own labels. Translations are mine and kept close. A note on the book's standing. It is the second of the Rebbe's graded manuals. It follows Chovat HaTalmidim, which was written for boys, and it was meant to prepare for a planned "Chovat HaAvrekhim". The introduction says only someone who has already worked through Chovat HaTalmidim should read it (line 20).

family: The Piaseczner Rebbe: the inner meditative world
title: Mevo HaShe'arim: the inner meditative world
abstract: Title page (lines 1-6). Named as gate one of Chovat HaAvreichim, for those who have finished the earlier two books. Ch. 1 (lines 7-95): what a prophet really was. A prophet was not mainly a fortune-teller or a moral preacher. Prophecy was a level of service: the body refined until it becomes soul, so that nothing separates the person from the holy. God wants all Israel to be prophets. The "work of prophecy" continues now, even though prophecy itself has ended.

family: The Piaseczner Rebbe: the inner meditative world
title: Tzav VeZeruz: the inner meditative world
abstract: 1 (lines 1-2). Why keep a notebook: life is too short to live the corrected life; writing yourself down lets your soul's rises and falls live on in the readers who "swallow" it. 2 (line 3). Each year, picture the person you mean to be next year, "the imagined Reuven," and measure yourself against him. 3 (line 4). When your heart feels broken, do not trust it yet; it may only be a lack of some desire. Hurry in while the heart is open. 4 (lines 5-19).

family: The classic works read as contemplation
title: The Tanya, Likkutei Amarim: a meditative reading
abstract: Likkutei Amarim walks a person from the inside of their own chest to the purpose of the whole world, and back into their hands. It starts where people actually are: split. A good impulse and a selfish one in the same hour, a prayer that moves you and fades by lunch. It names two souls, one of them "truly a part of God above" (line 86), and it refuses to let the struggle mean failure.

family: The classic works read as contemplation
title: The Tanya, Shaar HaYichud to the end: a meditative reading
abstract: This half of the Tanya walks a person from the head, down through the heart, into the hand, and ends in silence. It is a road, not a lecture. Read slowly, it does to a mind what it describes. It starts with a child. Chinukh Katan, 'a small education', opens with the verse 'Train a child in his way'. It says there are two loves of God. One is a flame that rises by itself, a gift.

family: The classic works read as contemplation
title: The Gate of Unity: a meditative reading
abstract: The Gate of Unity walks a person from the edge of their own mind down a long ladder to the ground under their feet, and finds the same One on every rung. It calls itself "the tract on contemplation" (line 3), and it begins not with God but with how to look: a strong, unhurried gaze that stays on one idea until it knows its depth (line 10), like a river with its breadth, length and depth (lines 16-23), with the mind gathered into one point (line 52).

family: The classic works read as contemplation
title: Imrei Binah: a meditative reading
abstract: Imrei Binah is one long walk through a single verse and the two mitzvot bound to it. "Hear, O Israel, Havayah is our God, Havayah is One": the book asks what happens when a person says it, and it keeps asking for six hundred columns. It begins by clearing the table.

family: The classic works read as contemplation
title: Kuntres HaHitpa'alut: a meditative reading
abstract: Kuntres HaHitpa'alut, the Tract on Ecstasy, walks a person from a soul asleep to a soul that sings without hearing itself sing. It is two letters of the Mitteler Rebbe to the chassidim, written in 5574 (1813/14). The first letter begins with sleep: worry over a living has emptied minds and hearts, and the Mitteler Rebbe calls that distraction "the exile of the Shechinah" and "sleep" (line 12).

family: The classic works read as contemplation
title: Hemshech Samach Vav, first half: a meditative reading
abstract: Hemshech Samach Vav is not a book you read once. It is a year of Shabbat and festival talks, given by the Rebbe Rashab from Rosh Hashanah 5666 (1905) onward, that keep circling one question until the reader is changed by it. This half of it walks through forty-five maamarim, from the first Rosh Hashanah to the Shemini Atzeret a year later.

family: The classic works read as contemplation
title: Hemshech Samach Vav, second half: a meditative reading
abstract: The first half of Hemshech Samach Vav asked why there are worlds at all, and answered: a desire with no reason, that the Essence of God be at home below. This second half asks the next question, the one a person lives with. If that is what He wants, what in me reaches Him? Not His light, which the Rashab has already shown can be known and felt and ranked. Him.

family: The classic works read as contemplation
title: Kuntres HaAvodah and Kuntres HaTefillah: a meditative reading
abstract: These two small books answer one question the Rashab's chassidim kept asking him: how do you pray? Kuntres HaTefillah (1900) opens with it in so many words: "each one of our people asks and seeks: how does one pray?" (Tefillah line 41). Kuntres HaAvodah, written ten years later, is the long answer.

family: The classic works read as contemplation
title: Sefer HaArachim, vol. 9, Achdus Hashem: a meditative reading
abstract: This volume is not a maamar or a book of chapters. It is an encyclopedia entry, a very long one, built from hundreds of sources in Chassidus and the Rebbe's talks. Yet read in order it walks a person down a real road: from the word 'one' said without thinking, to the Essence present as Himself in the plainest things, with the world still standing.

family: The classic works read as contemplation
title: Sha'arei HaYichud VeEmunah: a meditative reading
abstract: This book is one long climb and one long return. R. Aharon of Strashelye, the Alter Rebbe's closest student, takes the whole map of the Kabbalah (sefirot, faces, lights and vessels, smallness and greatness) and uses every piece of it to say one sentence: as He was alone before the worlds were made, so He is alone now. Read slowly, the map stops being a diagram of heaven and becomes a way of seeing the room you are sitting in.

family: The map of consciousness and meditation in Chassidus
title: The map of consciousness and meditation in Chassidus
abstract: The guide used to walk everyone through the same eight steps. The owner's call (D34): the guide should know the whole territory, place the person on it each turn from what they say, and take the next real step from wherever they are, in whatever direction the conversation opens. This file is that territory. It has 86 states (nodes), 241 movements between them (edges), and 8 currents that every movement serves. It is never shown or named to the person.

family: Sitting with the One: a meditation manual
title: Sitting with the One: a meditation manual
abstract: Chassidus says G-d's oneness can't be understood, only glimpsed, and the glimpse comes in contemplation (hisbonenus): thinking one truth through, slowly, until it is as real to you as something you see. People don't come looking for G-d. They come looking for themselves, and in finding their true self they find Him. So the manual starts with you, climbs the rungs of the oneness, and comes back down into your day.

family: Sitting with the One: a meditation manual
title: Part I. How to Sit
abstract: Every instruction ends with a short bracket naming its source. Under most instructions a small Source note gives the line itself in Hebrew, copied from the text and checked with find_he.py verify at the line given. Only lines that came back FOUND are here. The file behind each short name is listed at the end ("Where the lines are"). Where we add something the sources don't say, such as a number of minutes, we say so and mark it (ours).

family: Sitting with the One: a meditation manual
title: Part II · The ladder of sittings
abstract: Fourteen sittings, in order. Each one takes one face of a single truth, that there is nothing besides God, even here, and gives it to you as something to sit with: one line, a way to think it through, a picture, words to say, and one thing to do today. You go up the ladder from what is nearest (yourself), through the world and the rungs of the unity, as far up as anyone can reach, and then back down into your kitchen, your habits and your hands.

family: Sitting with the One: a meditation manual
title: Part III · Programs
abstract: The sittings are in Part II. This part is about when, how long, and how to tell whether any of it is working. Two sentences from the Tanya stand behind all of it. Stay with a thought "as far as your mind can grasp, and as your free time allows." And: "when he trains himself this way constantly, the habit becomes nature."

family: Sitting with the One: a meditation manual
title: Part IV. What Happens Inside
abstract: This is a description, not a checklist. The states below come in roughly this order for many people, but not for everyone, and not every sitting. Some come on the first day and some after years. Some never come in a way you can name, and the sources say that the deepest ones are the least felt. So read it before or after a sitting, never during. During the sitting your job is the line (Part I).

family: Sitting with the One: a meditation manual
title: Part V. When It's Hard
abstract: First, one line about danger. If what you're carrying is real danger (thoughts of harming yourself or not wanting to be here, someone hurting or controlling you, fear of hurting someone, not eating or functioning at all, or racing, sleepless certainty about a special mission), stop the sitting. This isn't a meditation problem. The guide follows its crisis protocol and nothing else: it says plainly that this needs a person now, and helps you reach one (the guide's constitution, SAFETY). Everything below is for everything else.

family: How Jewish meditation works: techniques, method and mechanism
title: Meditative techniques in Chassidus and the Kabbalah it draws on: a catalogue
abstract: The corpus holds 39 distinct techniques (not counting letter permutation, which ABULAFIA.md covers), in seven families, plus one recorded absence: no breathing technique exists in these sources (B6). Chabad hisbonenus is one of them, the constructive family's centre, and the earlier research covers it well.

family: How Jewish meditation works: techniques, method and mechanism
title: Abulafia: how meditation works, from the man who wrote the method down
abstract: Four marks run through the file: - Attested: a text I read says it. The source and line are given. - Reported: a scholar (Scholem, Idel, Kaplan) says it, and I could not read the text myself. Unverified here. - Reconstructed: a reasonable filling-in of a gap. Not in any text. - Ours: this index's own reading or proposal.

family: How Jewish meditation works: techniques, method and mechanism
title: How it works: the science of Jewish and Chassidic meditation
abstract: Who it is for. The builders and the owner. It is written for a smart reader who is not a scientist: every technical term is explained the first time it appears. It is not the guide's voice. Like the psychology files, nothing here should reach a person as vocabulary. The guide never speaks in therapy or neuroscience terms (FOUNDATIONS §1). It explains mechanism, not truth.

family: How Jewish meditation works: techniques, method and mechanism
title: The meditative technology: a working manual for the guide
abstract: Aryeh Kaplan, reporting on his work with a circle of clinicians, said the texts give the ingredients of Jewish meditation but leave out "the means of mixing them together" (the owner's note, Aryeh Kaplan/threads/07). This file is an attempt at the means of mixing, for one setting: a text conversation in which the meditation and the knowing of the unity are the same act.

family: The Tanya as a book of consciousness
title: The Tanya as a book of consciousness · Part 1: the author's introduction and Likkutei Amarim chapters 1 to 18
abstract: This part reads the doorway of the Tanya and its first eighteen chapters as a map of the inner life. The title page promises that the whole of serving G-d is "very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, to do it," and these chapters show the ground under that promise. They begin where a person really is: pulled two ways, judging himself by a score, swinging between sadness and carelessness.

family: The Tanya as a book of consciousness
title: The Tanya as a book of consciousness · Part 2: Likkutei Amarim, chapters 19 to 35
abstract: This part of the Tanya goes under the thinking mind and then comes back up into the working day. Chapters 19 to 22 find the deepest layer a person has: a pull toward G-d that is older than any reason, a self that wants to go quiet in its source, and the plain truth that makes that pull make sense, that before the One everything is as nothing and the only real distance is feeling yourself a thing of your own.

family: The Tanya as a book of consciousness
title: The Tanya as a book of consciousness · Part 3: Likkutei Amarim, chapters 36 to 53
abstract: This part of the Tanya turns from the inner war to its purpose, and then to the states of the heart that carry a person through a day of service. It opens with a way of seeing this coarse, dark world as the very place the One wants to live (36), and a way of feeling a plain deed, a coin, a spoken word, lift your life up to Him (37).

family: The Tanya as a book of consciousness
title: The Tanya as a book of consciousness · Part 4: The Gate of Unity and the Letter on Return
abstract: This part holds two short books. Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah, the Gate of Unity and Faith, opens with a small preface called Chinuch Katan, "a small training," and then gives twelve chapters that take one state apart piece by piece: the state in which the world seems to stand on its own, and the state in which a person sees through it to the word that is saying it right now.

family: The Tanya as a book of consciousness
title: The Tanya as a book of consciousness · Part 5: Iggeret HaKodesh, letters 1 to 16
abstract: The Iggeret HaKodesh (the Holy Letters) are real letters, sent by the Alter Rebbe to his Chassidim over many years: thanks for Talmud finished, a warning after his release from prison, appeals for the poor and for the Land of Israel. Read as a map of consciousness, they are the part of the Tanya where the inner states meet the hand and the purse.

family: The Tanya as a book of consciousness
title: The Tanya as a book of consciousness · Part 6: Iggeret HaKodesh 17 to 32 and Kuntres Acharon
abstract: These are the last pages of the Tanya, and here the states of consciousness come inside letters about money, prayer, grief and quarrels in shul. The Holy Letters 17 to 32 keep returning to one movement: a heart that wakes below wakes something above. Mercy for a poor man opens mercy on you. Giving often, in small coins, lifts a fallen presence little by little. Love that splits between people makes the Shechinah sick; love that joins them lets life go round again.

family: The Tanya as a book of consciousness
title: The Tanya as a Meditation: pilot, Chapter 2
abstract: The Piaseczner Rebbe opens Hakhsharat HaAvrekhim by saying that the ways of the tzaddikim, the Kabbalists and the Baal Shem Tov's disciples "are the ways of the prophets of G-d" (1:2), and that "the first revelation in the holy ones was their own soul, the part of G-d above within them, revealed to them" (1:6). Chassidus, on this reading, is the prophetic path brought back: not ideas about G-d, but the experience that the prophets trained for.

family: The Tanya, reimagined
title: The Tanya, reimagined · Part 1: the opening and chapters 1-18
abstract: This part covers the book's doorway and its first long stretch. The title page and the compiler's foreword open it, told briefly, the way a friend might hand you a letter before you read the book it came with. Chapters 1-18 follow. They start where people really are, split between a pull toward the good and a pull toward the self. They name two souls, find a part of G-d under everything, and teach how the mind can hold a truth until the heart answers.

family: The Tanya, reimagined
title: The Tanya, reimagined · Part 2: Likkutei Amarim, chapters 19-35
abstract: This part of the book goes down under the mind and then comes back up into the day. Chapters 19-22 find a love in the soul that is older than any reason, a flame that leans home, and then give the book's own plain statement of the unity: before Him everything is as nothing, His word never leaves Him, and the only real separation is feeling yourself a thing of your own.

family: The Tanya, reimagined
title: The Tanya, reimagined · Part 3: chapters 36-53
abstract: This part is the book coming down from its summit. Chapter 33 asked you to see that He alone fills this very place. Now the book asks what that is for, and its answer is plain and startling: the purpose of everything is this lowest, darkest world, where light will shine out of darkness (36). From there it turns practical. Deeds lift the world, and charity lifts a whole life (37).

family: The Tanya, reimagined
title: The Tanya, reimagined · Part 4: The Gate of Unity and the Letter on Return
abstract: This part carries two short books of the Tanya. The first is Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah, the Gate of Unity and Faith, which opens with a small introduction called Chinuch Katan, "a small education." It takes the world in front of you, the sky, the table, a stone, and shows it being spoken right now by the word that made it. Then it walks the mind up to its own wall, where only faith goes on, and back down again to the stone.

family: The Tanya, reimagined
title: The Tanya, reimagined · Part 5: Iggeret HaKodesh (the Holy Epistle), letters 1-16
abstract: The Iggeret HaKodesh is not a book the Alter Rebbe sat down to write. It is a bundle of real letters, sent over many years to his Chassidim in their towns: letters of thanks, letters of warning, letters asking for money for the poor and for the Holy Land, one written just after he came home from prison in Petersburg. So they sound different from the chapters before them. They are shorter, warmer, more urgent, and they almost always end in the hand: pray longer, answer softly, give.

family: The Tanya, reimagined
title: The Tanya, reimagined · Part 6: Iggeret HaKodesh 17-32 and Kuntres Acharon
abstract: These are the last pages of the Tanya. The Holy Letters were written by the Alter Rebbe to his Chassidim over many years and gathered by his sons after his passing. Most are short. They ask people to give charity, to pray with care, to stop talking in shul, to love one another, and they comfort people who have lost a teacher.

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: The full depth — digest of the readings
abstract: Hemshech Ayin Beis, lines 1-1950 (Shavuos 5672 to Shavuos 5674). Its main addition to the depth: under every light of the soul it finds one plain point, and it shows that the deepest point is the lowest and easiest to reach. (1) Will is under love. Love has reasons and limits; the soul's will for G-d has none, not even pleasure. It is the bond, like a father's will for his son. It stays when love is gone and rules over every pleasure.

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: FULL DESCENT: the whole depth, station by station
abstract: The full depth of Chassidus does not stop at 'there is nothing but Him'; that sentence is where the real descent starts. First you notice that you, too, are being made right now and given a place, not erased. Then you find that even your humility and your love still have a 'me' inside them, and that the deeper quiet cannot be made, only given or found.

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: AB1: Hemshech Ayin Beis, lines 1-1950
abstract: This slice runs from Shavuos 5672 to the second night of Shavuos 5674. It is mostly long, technical Kabbalah: Tohu and Tikkun, Keser and the hidden Chochmah, the incense and the offerings. Through all of it, the Rebbe Rashab keeps finding one plain point under each light of the soul. He also keeps showing that the deepest point is the lowest one, and the easiest to reach.

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: AB2: Hemshech Ayin Beis (Rebbe Rashab), lines 1951-3900, read for the full depth
abstract: The Rebbe Rashab in this stretch of the Hemshech is a master of the inside of avodah. The ideas (or and kli, tzimtzum, screens, Atzilus and BYA) are the frame; again and again he stops to say what it is like in a person, often in Yiddish, and where a person goes wrong. What it adds to 'Go deeper': Knowing is not yet seeing. Understanding shines only while you think; then 'the love passes and goes'. Seeing stays, like a beautiful thing you once saw.

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: AB3: Hemshech Ayin Beis, lines 3901-5750
abstract: What this slice is. Hemshech Ayin Beis, lines 3901-5750: the second part (the maamarim of Shavuos 5672 through Vayera 5673, said aloud) and the long written continuation (Ein od; three sweetenings; truth and the Talmud; letters of the soul; souls and angels; "black am I and beautiful"; the lamp; Kel De'os). The Rebbe Rashab keeps one question in front of him: how does the hidden Essence itself, not just its light, come down into a person, a body and a dark world?

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: AR: the Alter Rebbe's depths (Torah Ohr, Likkutei Torah, Tanya)
abstract: The Alter Rebbe's maamarim go deeper by being honest about the self. Even the greatest lover of G-d is 'something, not nothing' (Tanya 35); even Rabbi Akiva's death on the word 'One' was a creature's yielding, 'still far from G-dliness' until a light from above took it in (TO Vayeshev); and yielding itself can turn into pride (LT Behar). So the bottom is not a feeling and not an achievement.

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: MH: the Rebbe Maharash and the Rebbe Rayatz, read for 'Go deeper'
abstract: The two Rebbeim of this slice keep asking one question that DESCENT left open: what kind of 'nothing' is meant, where is it true, and who can reach it? Their answers push the depth downward and inward, not higher. 'Nothing' has two meanings. From His side, the world comes from a ray that takes no room, so nothing in Him changed. From our side, 'nothing' means what we cannot grasp, like our own soul: nearer than anything, certain, never seen.

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: MR1: the Mitteler Rebbe's core works, read for the full depth
abstract: The Mitteler Rebbe writes for people who do not feel. His books say so. Derech Chaim was written because of 'the great poverty and pressure of the hour,' for people who 'cannot free even one hour,' so that 'every man will find rest for his soul according to his place.' Kuntres HaHitpa'alut is a long diagnosis of real versus imitation arousal.

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: MR2: Toras Chaim (the Mitteler Rebbe), read for the full depth
abstract: The Mitteler Rebbe's Toras Chaim (on Bereishis and Shemos) climbs slowly and at great length: each maamar lays foundation upon foundation until the reader stands inside the idea. What it adds to 'Go deeper': (1) two bittuls, not one: setting yourself aside versus finding you were never apart (the one who stands before the King always, 'like a silent stone'), and each bittul is a 'something' before the next.

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: MR3: The Mitteler Rebbe, read for depth (Maamarei Admur HaEmtzai, Sha'arei Teshuvah, Ner Mitzvah VeTorah Or)
abstract: The Mitteler Rebbe adds four things to the full depth. (1) The deepest point is a PLACE and a REST, not an experience: the yechida rests in the four cubits, in plain bodily Shabbos rest, where great and simple are equal; the true Being rests only in plain being.

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: RB: the Lubavitcher Rebbe, read for the full depth
abstract: The other Rebbeim teach that there is nothing but Him. The Lubavitcher Rebbe's maamarim keep asking one more question past that point, and his answers move the depth in five directions that DESCENT does not yet have. Past 'nullified' to 'no second'. The Rebbe climbs past bitul itself. Speech yields to thought like a chariot to its rider; thought dissolves into the idea; but 'in your heart, only One' means there is no existence besides Him, not even one that is nullified to Him (RB-C05).

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: RK: The Rebbe Rashab's short works, read through for the full depth
abstract: The Rebbe Rashab's short works add the inside of the climb: how a person actually gets from knowing 'nothing but Him' to living it, and why it so often fails. Five findings. (1) The hiding is His. Nature is not water over a sunk thing; He made the cover, so G-d in nature is G-d beyond nature, and solidity itself is made of His hiding, which is His kindness (Umaayan 23-25). (2) Near is quiet.

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: RM: the Rebbe Rashab's Sefer HaMaamarim, read for depth
abstract: The Rebbe Rashab's Sefer HaMaamarim (all years, OCR) takes the depth below 'nothing but Him' in four directions. First, the self: the soul is not a ray that vanishes but His essence become someone, like a child from a father; even yechidah is only a name, and under it is the 'true Something'.

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: SV1 · Samach Vav, lines 1-3100: the depth as the Rashab climbs it
abstract: The first third of Samach Vav (Rosh Hashana to Sivan 5666) is the Rebbe Rashab's long argument about why there is a world and what reaches G-d's Essence. Read through, it does not climb only upward. It climbs to the Essence and then insists, again and again, that the Essence is found lowest: in the plain physical mitzvah, in teshuvah from the bottom, in the day after prayer. Seven things it adds to "Go deeper" (all stated):

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: SV2: Hemshech Samach Vav, lines 3101-6200 (OCR)
abstract: Hemshech Samach Vav, lines 3101-6200 (OCR), runs from Shavuos 5666 to Shemos 5668. It reads like one long argument about who reaches G-d's Essence and how. The answer keeps turning upside down. Feeling G-d in prayer is good. The child who runs after a hidden father is deeper. The plain servant who serves under the yoke, with no light, no knowing and no love, only because he was told to, is deeper still: he is 'not a being for himself', and his work counts as the Master's own hand.

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: SV3 · Samach Vav, the ending and the key (lines 6201-9229)
abstract: This slice is the end of Samach Vav and a key to the whole of it. It holds the close of the last maamar (Vaera 5668) and its completion on Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur and Shabbos; the Rashab's own notes; the Rebbe Rayatz's explanations of the opening; and a printed summary of all 61 maamarim (the publishers' 'content, chapter heads and summary'; its author is not named in the slice).

family: The full depth: reading the Rebbeim through
title: TZ: the Tzemach Tzedek, read for depth
abstract: The Tzemach Tzedek adds three things to the full depth. First, he takes the ladder into the act of addressing G-d: no name reaches the Essence; only 'You' (Atah), said face to face, does; we pray to Him, never to His attributes; of the Essence the right word is not even 'One' but 'Alone', while 'One' is His oneness inside a world that is really there. Second, he shows that the bottom is not calm.

family: Lights, vessels, and the path of prophecy
title: ON: Ontology. What the unity is, at its deepest
abstract: The owner asked for the unity at its deepest: what it is, not only how it feels. Four findings. The Tzemach Tzedek already wrote the ladder. In Derech Mitzvosecha, the mitzvah to know that G-d is one is read on three levels, and he says so. First, the plain meaning: no created thing has rule of its own (ON-01). Second, the Zohar's meaning: 'Havayah is Elokim', the name hidden in nature is one with the name above nature (ON-02).

family: Lights, vessels, and the path of prophecy
title: AN: Anthropology. The human being as the place of the unity
abstract: The question. Where does the unity of G-d happen? The sources' answer is: in a human being. Not mainly in the heavens, and not only in the mind, but in a person with a body, two pulls, and a choice. This file lays out the sources' picture of that person, so the guide knows who it is talking to. The deepest self is already one with Him. A part of every Jewish soul is "literally a part of G-d above", breathed from His inside (AN-01).

family: Lights, vessels, and the path of prophecy
title: DESCENT: past 'there is nothing but Him'
abstract: The owner's complaint: tapping 'Go deeper' stops at 'there's only Him' and then slides into integration and 'pick a specific object'. The sources do not stop there. They go on in a clear order: into the self, through the self's own disappearance (which cannot be made), to the edge of 'nothing' and past it, to the point in the soul that was never apart, to the bond that cannot be let go. And then they turn: the bottom sends you back, and the way back is the deeper half.

family: Lights, vessels, and the path of prophecy
title: GM: Guided meditations in the teachers' voices
abstract: The owner asked for sittings that feel like entering a sacred chamber with the wisest teachers of Chassidus, before the Master of all mysteries. This file gives the guide seven ways in, one per master, each with its own door. Each master guided an inner act differently, and the differences are usable. The Baal Shem Tov (as his teachings were collected) brings you in through awe and joy. He allows the small day: "He fills the earth and He is near me" is already "great cleaving".

family: Lights, vessels, and the path of prophecy
title: PC: Chassidus as the continuation of prophecy, and the bridge
abstract: The owner's sentence is in the sources, almost word for word. The Piaseczner says it outright: the ways of the tzaddikim of Kabbalah and of the Baal Shem Tov's chassidim "are the ways of the prophets of God" (Hakhsharat HaAvrekhim 1:2). And his central claim is sharper than "continuation": prophecy ended, but "the work of prophecy continues even now" (Mevo HaShe'arim 1:25). He defines that work as removing the border between holy and ordinary, until the body too becomes soul. Stated.

family: Lights, vessels, and the path of prophecy
title: PK: The path of prophecy, reconstructed from the sources Kaplan used
abstract: stated = a source says it. ours = our synthesis. Each entry also says which parts of its stage are attested (a text describes it) and which are reconstructed (inferred, by Kaplan or by us).

family: Lights, vessels, and the path of prophecy
title: PS — Psychology: how the unity is held in consciousness
abstract: The question. The other strands say what the unity is (ON) and who receives it (AN). This one asks: how does an idea about G-d become something a person actually lives in? And what goes wrong on the way? The arc, in plain words. The sources give a clear path. It runs from mind to heart to hand. The goal is a transparent self, not a vanished one. The Rashab says the vessel that can receive light is specifically bittul hayesh: a self that exists and yields.

family: Lights, vessels, and the path of prophecy
title: The Depth Engine: how Chassidus takes any idea deeper
abstract: A maamar deepens by a small set of repeated turns, and they are marked in the text. The same phrases recur across two hundred years: "and this needs understanding", "the matter is", "to understand this we must first lay down", "but in truth", "and higher still", "the parable is not like the thing", "both are true", "the point of the explanation", "and from this is understood", "specifically". Each does one job to an idea. Seventeen such jobs are written up below as moves M1-M17. The question is the engine.

family: Lights, vessels, and the path of prophecy
title: VS · Vessels: making a person safe and open enough to receive
abstract: The sources have a word for this, and a rule. The Mitteler Rebbe writes that light has no hold except in a vessel, and the more the vessel widens, the more light it holds. Without a vessel, being moved is "a flame flying in the air". His main vessel is plain: take it on and do something at once. So the first design rule is simple. Every sitting has a small deed chosen before it and done after it. (VS-01)

family: The inner world of Achdus Hashem
title: The inner world of Achdus Hashem: a map, and the conversation as a Chassidic prayer
abstract: What this world is. It is a whole world, not one idea. Its centre is a lived sense: there is nothing but Him, and He is fully here. It has depths: thirteen deeper answers to the question "what does it mean that G-d is One?" (section 2). It has regions a person can actually be in, from the world turning transparent to the quiet after (section 3).

family: The inner world of Achdus Hashem
title: AR · The arc over time and into life
abstract: The other files map where a person can be: the 14 rungs (../ONE-PROCESS.md), the 86 states (../consciousness-map/MAP.md), the manual's sittings and its forty-day ladder course (../manual/part3-programs.md), its "real and counterfeit" (../manual/part4-inside.md) and its troubleshooting (../manual/part5-when-its-hard.md). This strand maps time: what happens to a person across weeks, months and years, and how the inside reaches the outside. Where those files already quote a source, this file cites them and adds what they lack.

family: The inner world of Achdus Hashem
title: BS: The wider Chassidic world on the inner experience of the unity
abstract: The Besht's centre is dveikus: a thread, not a peak. The mind keeps resting on Him while the hands work. It is trained in small things, comes and goes like fire, and its first fruit is equanimity (BS-01 to BS-03, BS-07). "No place empty of Him" is applied to the mind itself. Even the thought you drifted into is not outside Him; He is there "with His back turned" (Maggid). Even a pleasure has a spark you can follow home (Besht, Vitebsk).

family: The inner world of Achdus Hashem
title: Chassidic prayer as the place of integration
abstract: The owner: "In Chabad, prayer is the time to do this integration between the G-dly soul and the animal soul... We teach, show and explain to the animal soul that it doesn't need to be its own self, because the only true reality is G-d... This app, this conversation, will be a way of facilitating a Chassidic prayer: not necessarily the literal wording, but the psychological aspects of it."

family: The inner world of Achdus Hashem
title: EX: The experience itself, from inside
abstract: This extends, and does not repeat, consciousness-map/MAP.md (states S39-S78) and ONE-PROCESS.md (the 14 steps). MAP names states one by one. ONE-PROCESS gives the order. This file groups the states into regions a guide can lead someone into, and adds what the sources say each region feels like, plus how to tell it from its imitation. Each entry says which MAP states and steps it builds on.

family: The inner world of Achdus Hashem
title: GD: Guiding a modern person into the inner world, in a chat
abstract: Experiences close to this one are real, common, and partly learnable. Awe, self-transcendent experience, flow, the mystical "unity" reports and the felt presence of G-d share two features: less self in the way, and more connection (Yaden et al. 2017). People differ a lot in how easily they enter (absorption). Practice increases it. People enter by doing, not by hearing. The strongest finding for a guide is T. M.

family: The inner world of Achdus Hashem
title: The doors: how a person enters the lived unity
abstract: The map (consciousness-map/MAP.md) says where a person can be. The ladder (ONE-PROCESS.md) says how the rungs follow one another. This file says how a person gets in: the practical doors the sources name, each with its own key. (ours) A door is a concrete act, at a concrete time, that the sources say opens the experience of "nothing but Him, and He is fully here".

family: The inner world of Achdus Hashem
title: UN: the depths of the unity itself
abstract: The owner asked to take the unity of G-d deeper, map it through all of Chassidus, and explain it on a universal level. The index already has the rungs (FOUR-SOURCES.md: lower, higher, alone, and the world held), the twelve faces (SPINE.md), the ladder of contemplation (ONE-PROCESS.md) and the ten layers for anyone (universal-framework/FRAMEWORK.md).

family: How Chassidus reasons about the unity
title: One framework for thinking about the unity of G-d
abstract: The problem. The guide has learned the conclusions of Chassidus ("He gives you being right now", "there is nothing but Him") and pastes them onto any question. That is imitation. A maamar does something else. It raises a real question, sorts out what is being talked about, argues, gives a picture and admits where the picture fails, climbs to the point where the clash goes away, and then brings it down into something to do.

family: How Chassidus reasons about the unity
title: DEEP · How the later Rebbeim reason the unity at its deepest
abstract: The deep layer of Chabad, as the Tzemach Tzedek, the Rebbe Rashab and the Rebbe reason it, does not get its depth by climbing to a higher light. It gets it by changing the subject of the sentence. Almost every move begins by asking whether a claim is about G-d's light (a shining that shows Him without being Him, changes nothing in Him, and pushes out what is not itself) or about His Essence (which nothing hides, which negates nothing, and which is the self of each thing).

family: How Chassidus reasons about the unity
title: MR: How the Mitteler Rebbe reasons about the unity: a procedure
abstract: The Mitteler Rebbe (R. Dovber, 1773-1827) does not mainly argue that G-d is one. He teaches how a person comes to KNOW it, and how to tell whether he has. His three books on this are one method seen from three sides. The Gate of Unity (Shaar HaYichud, 1820) calls itself "the tract on contemplation" and gives the method and the map. Imrei Binah (1821) applies it to the Shema, where faith is meant to become knowing.

family: How Chassidus reasons about the unity
title: SHY: the Gate of Unity as a step-by-step proof
abstract: Shaar HaYichud VeHaEmunah (the Gate of Unity and Faith, Tanya part 2) is not a list of claims about G-d. It is a proof, built in order, where each chapter answers a question the last chapter left open. That is its mark. It starts with a purpose, not a thesis (Chinuch Katan): the love every person can reach is "made" by thinking, and the first thing to think about is His unity. Then it starts the proof from a word in a verse that seems too strong ("Know today...

family: The animal soul: how a G-dly idea reaches it
title: How Chassidus brings a G-dly idea to the animal soul: the merged catalogue
abstract: The animal soul can be taught, but it is a different listener. All six slices agree: it has a mind, so it can be shown things. But its mind is narrow. It is busy with its own good, its own life, and what it can see and touch. The G-dly soul needs little; the long work is for the animal soul. The Alter Rebbe says the long praises before Shema exist for it; the G-dly soul "has no need for so much contemplation" (AR05).

title: Methods for reaching the animal soul: the Alter Rebbe (slice AR)
